notes.front: What is a container?
notes.back: A running process that the operating system isolates and limits in resources, packaged with the files it needs to run.
notes.explanation: Containers on one machine share its operating system, so many more applications fit on the same hardware than with a separate machine or VM each.
notes.example: Three apps on one server, each in its own container, prevented by the operating system from interfering with the others.

notes.front: What is a container image?
notes.back: An immutable, static file holding everything needed to create a container: code, libraries, tools and settings.
notes.explanation: Images are built once and downloaded to run; one image can start as many containers as needed.
notes.example: A web server image downloaded to a developer’s laptop behaves the same as the copy running in the cloud.

notes.front: What is a container registry?
notes.back: A service that stores container images and lets people find and download them.
notes.explanation: Developers push the images they build to a registry; the machines that run them pull the images from it.
notes.example: A team pushes its web server image to a registry, and servers in three countries pull that same image to run it.
notes.source: NIST CSRC Glossary, “registry”, from NIST SP 800-190; Kubernetes documentation, “Images”

notes.front: What is containerisation (spelt “containerization” in the sources)?
notes.back: Packaging application code with the libraries and dependencies it needs into a single lightweight executable: a container image.
notes.explanation: The dependencies are listed in a file, so it can be kept under version control and the build can be automated.
notes.example: Turning a web app and all its libraries into one image that runs the same everywhere.

notes.front: In general, what is a runtime?
notes.back: Software that executes other software, translating a program’s commands into actions for the operating system.
notes.explanation: In cloud native contexts, the word usually refers to the software that runs containers, covered next.
notes.example: The program that actually starts your application and passes its requests on to the operating system.

notes.front: What is a container runtime?
notes.back: The software responsible for running containers: it gets images, unpacks them and runs them with isolated, allocated resources.
notes.explanation: Without it, each application would have to deal with the mechanics of every operating system itself.
notes.example: The program on a server that takes a downloaded image and starts it as an isolated container.

notes.front: What is the OCI (Open Container Initiative)?
notes.back: The initiative whose specifications standardise container images and container runtimes.
notes.explanation: Because of the standard, any OCI-compliant runtime can be combined with any OCI-compliant tool that manages containers.
notes.example: An image built with one vendor’s tools runs on another vendor’s runtime because both follow the OCI specifications.

notes.front: What is an image tag?
notes.back: A human-readable name after an image’s name that identifies a version, such as busybox:1.32.0; it can be moved to another image.
notes.explanation: Tags are convenient but mutable: the same tag can point to different software on different days.
notes.example: myapp:v1.0 or myapp:latest.

notes.front: What is a cryptographic hash?
notes.back: The fixed-length output of a hash function, which is built so that no two different inputs can practically give the same output.
notes.explanation: That makes a hash work like a fingerprint for data: compare two hashes to tell whether the data is exactly the same.
notes.example: Two files that differ by one letter give different hashes, so the hash tells them apart.
notes.source: NIST CSRC Glossary, “hash function”, from FIPS 186-5

notes.front: What is an image digest?
notes.back: A unique, immutable identifier for an image: a cryptographic hash of its content, such as sha256:1ff6…
notes.explanation: Any change to the image changes the digest, so referring to an image by digest always gives exactly the same content.
notes.example: If a tag is a nickname you can give to someone else, a digest is a fingerprint.
notes.source: Cloud Native Glossary (CNCF), “Image Digest”; Kubernetes documentation, “Images” (“hashes of the image’s content”)

notes.front: What is Kubernetes, in one sentence?
notes.back: A portable, extensible, open source platform for managing containerised workloads and services, supporting declarative configuration and automation.
notes.explanation: Containers package applications well, but in production something must restart, scale and connect them across many machines; Kubernetes does that.
notes.example: If a container goes down, Kubernetes starts another one without anyone having to step in.

notes.front: What is the kubelet?
notes.back: The Kubernetes agent on each node that makes sure the containers it has been given are running and healthy.
notes.explanation: It is the part of Kubernetes that asks the node’s container runtime to launch containers.
notes.example: A node is told to run a web server container; its kubelet has the runtime start it and keeps checking on it.

notes.front: What is a container’s imagePullPolicy?
notes.back: The setting that controls when the kubelet pulls (downloads) the container’s image: IfNotPresent, Always or Never.
notes.explanation: The pull policy and the image tag together decide when an image is fetched from the registry.
notes.example: With IfNotPresent, a node that already holds the image starts the container without downloading it again.

notes.front: What is the CRI (Container Runtime Interface)?
notes.back: The standard way the kubelet talks to whatever container runtime a node uses, so Kubernetes can work with many runtimes.
notes.explanation: Runtimes can be swapped without rebuilding any cluster components.
notes.example: Changing a node from one CRI runtime to another without rebuilding Kubernetes.

notes.front: What is containerd?
notes.back: A container runtime with an emphasis on simplicity, robustness and portability, running as a background service on Linux or Windows.
notes.explanation: It fetches and stores images, runs containers and gives them network access; Kubernetes supports it through the CRI.
notes.example: A node whose kubelet talks to containerd to start every container.

notes.front: What is CRI-O?
notes.back: An implementation of the CRI that lets Kubernetes use any container runtime compatible with the OCI runtime specification.
notes.explanation: It also fetches OCI images from remote registries.
notes.example: A cluster that uses CRI-O so that its kubelets can drive an OCI-compliant runtime.

notes.front: What is Docker Engine?
notes.back: Software for building and running containers, using features of the Linux kernel to keep them apart.
notes.explanation: Docker popularised the Linux containers pattern, though containers existed in Linux long before it.
notes.example: Building an image with “docker build” and running it with Docker on a laptop.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, Glossary, “Docker”; Kubernetes blog, “Updated: Dockershim Removal FAQ”

notes.front: What was the dockershim?
notes.back: A component of Kubernetes, up to version 1.23, that let the kubelet talk to Docker Engine.
notes.explanation: Docker Engine does not implement the CRI, so this special code bridged the gap; it was always meant to be temporary.
notes.example: Like a temporary travel adapter: the kubelet spoke one language (the CRI), Docker Engine another, and the shim translated between them.

notes.front: What is a RuntimeClass?
notes.back: A Kubernetes feature for selecting the container runtime configuration used to run containers.
notes.explanation: It lets you balance performance against security, or run the same runtime with different settings.
notes.example: Sensitive containers run in a runtime that uses hardware virtualisation for extra isolation, at some extra overhead.

notes.front: What is a cgroup (control group)?
notes.back: A Linux kernel feature that groups processes and limits, accounts for and isolates their use of CPU, memory, disk and network.
notes.explanation: The kubelet and the container runtime use cgroups to enforce the resources containers may use.
notes.example: A cap that stops one container’s processes using more than their share of a node’s memory.

notes.front: What are container lifecycle hooks?
notes.back: Events in a container’s management lifecycle that let you run code when they happen.
notes.explanation: Kubernetes exposes two: one just after a container is created and one just before it is terminated.
notes.example: Running a clean-shutdown script just before a container is stopped.

notes.front: What are container environment variables?
notes.back: Name=value pairs that give a running container useful information.
notes.explanation: They can come from the container image or from the definition you give Kubernetes.
notes.example: LOG_LEVEL=debug set for a container so the application logs more detail.

notes.front: On Linux and similar systems, who is root?
notes.back: The superuser: the account allowed to control and administer the system, doing things ordinary users may not.
notes.explanation: Because root can do almost anything, a program running as root that gets compromised is far more dangerous than one running as an ordinary user.
notes.example: Changing system-wide settings needs root; an ordinary user who tries is refused.
notes.source: NIST CSRC Glossary, “root user” and “superuser”, from CNSSI 4009-2022

notes.front: What is a Linux user namespace?
notes.back: A Linux kernel feature that lets a non-root user emulate superuser (root) privileges.
notes.explanation: It is used for “rootless containers” and limits the damage if an attacker breaks out of a container.
notes.example: A container that believes it runs as root while, outside it, it has only an ordinary user’s rights.

notes.front: What do containers on the same machine share?
notes.back: The machine’s operating system and its resources.
notes.explanation: Sharing spreads the operating system’s overhead, but it also means containers are less isolated than separate machines.

notes.front: Why must administrators limit the memory and CPU that containers use?
notes.back: Containers share resources, so without limits one container can make other applications perform poorly.
notes.explanation: Limits guarantee each application its share of the machine.

notes.front: How should you change the code of a containerised application that is already running?
notes.back: Build a new image that includes the change, then recreate the container from it.
notes.explanation: Containers are intended to be stateless and immutable: you do not change the code of a running container.

notes.front: Where are container images typically stored?
notes.back: In container registries, from which they are downloaded and run.
notes.explanation: You usually build an image of your application and push it to a registry before Kubernetes uses it.
notes.source: Cloud Native Glossary (CNCF), “Container Image”; Kubernetes documentation, “Images”

notes.front: Which standard schema must a container image follow?
notes.back: The one defined by the Open Container Initiative (OCI).
notes.explanation: The OCI Image Specification also defines the format of image digests.

notes.front: How does containerisation remove configuration drift?
notes.back: Containers always start from their image, so every restart resets them to the same initial state.
notes.explanation: Virtual machines, by contrast, can drift from their original configuration over time.

notes.front: In the traditional deployment era, what went wrong when several applications shared one physical server?
notes.back: There were no resource boundaries, so one application could take most of the resources and starve the others.
notes.explanation: Giving each application its own server fixed this but wasted resources and cost too much.

notes.front: What did the virtualised deployment era bring?
notes.back: Several isolated VMs on one physical server, giving better resource use, easier scaling and security between applications.
notes.explanation: Each VM is a full machine, running its own operating system on virtualised hardware.

notes.front: Why are containers considered lightweight compared with virtual machines?
notes.back: They relax isolation so that applications share the operating system, instead of each carrying its own.
notes.explanation: Like a VM, a container still has its own filesystem, share of CPU and memory, and process space.

notes.front: In the diagram, what does each virtual machine carry that each container does not?
notes.back: Its own operating system.
notes.explanation: Containers share the host’s operating system through the container runtime; each VM runs a full operating system on the hypervisor.

image.alt: Three stacks side by side. Traditional deployment: apps on one operating system on hardware. Virtualised deployment: hardware, operating system, hypervisor, then virtual machines, each with its own operating system, libraries and apps. Container deployment: hardware, operating system, container runtime, then containers, each with only its libraries and app.

notes.front: In the diagram, which layer sits between the operating system and the containers, where virtual machines have a hypervisor?
notes.back: The container runtime.
notes.explanation: The hypervisor carves up hardware for VMs; the container runtime runs containers on one shared operating system.

image.alt: Three stacks side by side. Traditional deployment: apps on one operating system on hardware. Virtualised deployment: hardware, operating system, hypervisor, then virtual machines, each with its own operating system, libraries and apps. Container deployment: hardware, operating system, container runtime, then containers, each with only its libraries and app.

notes.front: Why are containers portable across clouds and operating system distributions?
notes.back: They carry everything they need and do not depend on the machine under them.
notes.explanation: The same container runs on a laptop as it does in the cloud.

notes.front: Which technology, the subject of this topic, heads the CNCF definition’s list of typical cloud native technologies?
notes.back: Containers.
notes.explanation: The definition’s list is non-exhaustive; microservices, immutable infrastructure and serverless are also on it.
notes.source: CNCF Cloud Native Definition v1.1 (CNCF Technical Oversight Committee), “Definition”

notes.front: If an image name has no tag, which tag does Kubernetes assume?
notes.back: latest.
notes.explanation: Tags identify versions in a series of images; without one, Kubernetes uses :latest.

notes.front: If an image name has no registry hostname, which registry does Kubernetes assume?
notes.back: The Docker public registry.
notes.explanation: You can change this default in the container runtime’s configuration.

notes.front: Which full image reference does plain “busybox” stand for?
notes.back: docker.io/library/busybox:latest.
notes.explanation: With no registry and no tag, Kubernetes uses the Docker public registry and the latest tag.

notes.front: If an image reference has both a tag and a digest, which is used for pulling?
notes.back: Only the digest.
notes.explanation: For example, registry.k8s.io/pause:3.5@sha256:… is pulled by its digest.

notes.front: Which can be moved to point at a different image: a tag or a digest?
notes.back: A tag. Digests are fixed.
notes.explanation: A digest is a hash of the image’s content, so it cannot refer to anything else.

notes.front: Why should you avoid the :latest tag when deploying containers in production?
notes.back: It is harder to track which version is running, and harder to roll back properly.
notes.explanation: Use a meaningful tag such as v1.42.0, a digest, or both.

notes.front: What does imagePullPolicy IfNotPresent do?
notes.back: Pulls the image only if it is not already present on the node.
notes.explanation: A node that already holds the image starts the container without contacting the registry.

notes.front: What does imagePullPolicy Always do?
notes.back: Every time the kubelet launches a container, it asks the runtime to pull the image, resolving the name to a digest.
notes.explanation: Layers already cached are not downloaded again, so Always stays efficient while the registry is reachable.

notes.front: What does imagePullPolicy Never do?
notes.back: The kubelet never fetches the image; if it is not already on the node, the container fails to start.
notes.explanation: It suits nodes whose images are loaded in advance.

notes.front: imagePullPolicy is omitted and the image is given by digest. Which policy is set automatically?
notes.back: IfNotPresent.
notes.explanation: A digest always means the same content, so there is no need to pull again.

notes.front: imagePullPolicy is omitted and the image tag is :latest. Which policy is set automatically?
notes.back: Always.
notes.explanation: The :latest tag can point to new content at any time, so it is always checked.

notes.front: imagePullPolicy is omitted and the image has no tag at all. Which policy is set automatically?
notes.back: Always.
notes.explanation: No tag means :latest, and :latest means Always. A common trap: it is not IfNotPresent.

notes.front: imagePullPolicy is omitted and the tag is something other than :latest, such as :v1.42.0. Which policy is set automatically?
notes.back: IfNotPresent.
notes.explanation: A specific version tag is expected to stay put, so an image already on the node is reused.

notes.front: If you later change an image’s tag to :latest, does the automatically set imagePullPolicy change to Always?
notes.back: No. The policy is set only when first created, and is not updated afterwards.
notes.explanation: You must change the pull policy yourself after creation.

notes.front: Where must a container runtime be installed in a cluster that Kubernetes manages?
notes.back: On each node, so the kubelet can launch containers there.
notes.explanation: Kubernetes requires a runtime that conforms to the CRI.

notes.front: When the kubelet connects to the container runtime through the CRI, which role does it play?
notes.back: It acts as a gRPC client of the runtime.
notes.explanation: The runtime must offer the addresses the kubelet connects to (its runtime and image services).

notes.front: Since Kubernetes v1.26, which version of the CRI API must a container runtime support?
notes.back: v1. If it does not, the kubelet will not register the node.
notes.explanation: Check the runtime supports CRI v1 before upgrading a node’s Kubernetes version.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Kubernetes docs as of that date

notes.front: Which two container runtimes does the Kubernetes glossary name as supported through the CRI?
notes.back: containerd and CRI-O.
notes.explanation: Kubernetes supports these and any other implementation of the CRI.

notes.front: How is Docker Engine used as the container runtime for Kubernetes today?
notes.back: Through the cri-dockerd adapter, which integrates Docker Engine with Kubernetes.
notes.explanation: Kubernetes no longer contains its own Docker integration, so the adapter supplies a CRI interface.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Kubernetes docs as of that date

notes.front: What is the default CRI socket for cri-dockerd?
notes.back: /run/cri-dockerd.sock.
notes.explanation: The kubelet connects to the runtime through a socket like this: a local connection point on the node.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Kubernetes docs as of that date

notes.front: In which Kubernetes version was the dockershim removed?
notes.back: v1.24. Its removal had been announced with v1.20.
notes.explanation: Version 1.23 was the last to include it.

notes.front: Why was the dockershim removed from Kubernetes?
notes.back: It was a temporary bridge that had become a heavy maintenance burden, and it blocked features that newer CRI runtimes support.
notes.explanation: Examples of those features are cgroups v2 and user namespaces.
notes.source: Kubernetes blog, “Updated: Dockershim Removal FAQ”, “Why was the dockershim removed from Kubernetes?”

notes.front: After the dockershim removal, do images built with “docker build” still work in Kubernetes?
notes.back: Yes. They work with all CRI implementations, exactly as before.
notes.explanation: The removal took out a code path to Docker Engine, not support for images Docker builds.
notes.source: Kubernetes blog, “Updated: Dockershim Removal FAQ”, “Will my existing container images still work?”

notes.front: Are Docker and containers the same thing?
notes.back: No. Docker popularised Linux containers, but containers existed long before it and the ecosystem is much broader.
notes.explanation: Standards like the OCI and the CRI let many tools replace or extend parts of Docker.
notes.source: Kubernetes blog, “Updated: Dockershim Removal FAQ”, “Are Docker and containers the same thing?”

notes.front: Besides choosing between runtimes, what else can a RuntimeClass do?
notes.back: Run the same container runtime with different settings.
notes.explanation: The available settings depend on the CRI implementation.

notes.front: Which two cgroup drivers can the kubelet and container runtime use?
notes.back: cgroupfs and systemd.
notes.explanation: systemd is the init system of many Linux distributions: the first process, which manages the rest. cgroupfs is the kubelet’s default; systemd is recommended when systemd is the init system, and for cgroup v2.

notes.front: Why must the kubelet and the container runtime use the same cgroup driver?
notes.back: Two different cgroup managers give two views of resources, which can make nodes unstable under resource pressure.
notes.explanation: If you set systemd as the kubelet’s cgroup driver, you must also set it for the runtime.

notes.front: When does the PostStart hook run?
notes.back: Immediately after a container is created, at the same time as the container’s main process.
notes.explanation: It may run before, during or after the main process starts, so it cannot be relied on to go first.

notes.front: When is the PreStop hook called?
notes.back: Immediately before a container is terminated, for example because someone deleted it through the API or the node ran short of resources.
notes.explanation: It must finish before Kubernetes tells the container to stop.

notes.front: Several applications run as isolated processes on one server, sharing its operating system, each with its own resource limits. What is each one running in?
notes.back: A container.
notes.explanation: The operating system isolates the processes and constrains their resources.

notes.front: A developer downloads a static, unchangeable file from a registry and starts three identical containers from it. What is the file?
notes.back: A container image.
notes.explanation: One image can create as many containers as you need.

notes.front: A team packages its application code, libraries and dependencies into one lightweight executable image. What is this process called?
notes.back: Containerisation.
notes.explanation: The result of containerising an application is a container image.

notes.front: Which piece of software on a node actually unpacks an image and runs it as an isolated container?
notes.back: The container runtime.
notes.explanation: The kubelet asks the runtime to do this; it does not run containers itself.

notes.front: A company runs every application on its own physical server so that no application can starve another of resources. Which deployment era does this belong to?
notes.back: The traditional deployment era.
notes.explanation: It avoided resource contention but left servers underused and was expensive to maintain.

notes.front: Applications share one operating system but each has its own filesystem, CPU share and process space, and runs the same on a laptop as in the cloud. Which deployment era is this?
notes.back: The container deployment era.
notes.explanation: Containers are like VMs with relaxed isolation, which makes them lightweight and portable.

notes.front: Every node must run exactly the same code for an image, even if someone later re-pushes the tag. How should the image be referenced?
notes.back: By its digest, for example image@sha256:….
notes.explanation: A tag can be moved at the registry, leaving a mix of old and new code; a digest pins the exact content.

notes.front: A production app uses image myapp:latest, and a bad version needs rolling back. Why is this harder than it should be?
notes.back: With :latest it is hard to tell which version is running or return to the previous one.
notes.explanation: A meaningful version tag or a digest makes the running version clear.

notes.front: You want Kubernetes to check the registry every time a container starts. Which imagePullPolicy should you set?
notes.back: Always.
notes.explanation: Omitting the policy and using :latest or no tag would also result in Always.

notes.front: A team built all its images with Docker and fears the dockershim removal broke them. What should you tell them?
notes.back: Their images still work: Docker-built images run on all CRI runtimes.
notes.explanation: Only Kubernetes’ direct integration with Docker Engine was removed.
notes.source: Kubernetes blog, “Updated: Dockershim Removal FAQ”, “Will my existing container images still work?”

notes.front: A cluster on Kubernetes v1.30 must keep Docker Engine as its node runtime. What does it need?
notes.back: The cri-dockerd adapter, which gives Docker Engine a CRI interface.
notes.explanation: The built-in dockershim was removed in v1.24.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Kubernetes docs as of that date

notes.front: containerd and CRI-O: what do they have in common?
notes.back: Both are container runtimes that Kubernetes can use through the CRI.
notes.explanation: containerd is a general runtime; CRI-O implements the CRI to drive OCI-compliant runtimes.

notes.front: Some containers handle highly sensitive data and need extra isolation. Which feature lets you run them in a runtime that uses hardware virtualisation?
notes.back: RuntimeClass.
notes.explanation: You trade some additional overhead for stronger isolation.

notes.front: A container runs as root inside, but outside it has only an ordinary user’s rights, limiting damage from a break-out. Which Linux feature is this?
notes.back: A user namespace.
notes.explanation: User namespaces let a non-root user emulate root, enabling rootless containers.

notes.front: What is the difference between a container image and a container?
notes.back: The image is the static, immutable package; the container is a running process created from it.
notes.explanation: One image can start many containers.
notes.contrast: The package on disk, versus the running process.

notes.front: What is the key difference between a virtual machine and a container?
notes.back: Each VM runs its own full operating system; containers share the host’s operating system.
notes.explanation: That makes containers lighter, at the cost of weaker isolation than VMs.
notes.contrast: An operating system each, versus one shared operating system.

notes.front: What is the difference between an image tag and an image digest?
notes.back: A tag is a movable, human-readable name; a digest is an immutable hash of the image’s content.
notes.explanation: A tag is like a nickname; a digest is like a fingerprint.
notes.contrast: Mutable name, versus fixed content hash.

notes.front: What was removed in Kubernetes v1.24: Docker, or the dockershim?
notes.back: The dockershim, Kubernetes’ built-in bridge to Docker Engine. Docker itself and Docker-built images still work.
notes.explanation: Docker Engine can still be the runtime through cri-dockerd.
notes.contrast: A Kubernetes component, versus a separate product.

notes.front: What is the difference between the kubelet and the container runtime?
notes.back: The kubelet is Kubernetes’ node agent, making sure the containers it is given are running; the runtime actually runs them.
notes.explanation: They talk to each other through the CRI.
notes.contrast: The node agent, versus the software that executes containers.
